notable_claims: Principles of academic freedom should apply to academic computer systems.
Personal files in home directories should have the same privacy protections as physical files in university-assigned offices or labs.
Suspension from a computer is a serious penalty requiring due process similar to formal disciplinary warnings.
The selection of newsgroups on academic sites should follow the same principles as library book and magazine selection.
classification.summary: Carl M. Kadie presents a draft framework to codify the application of academic freedom principles to university computer systems. The document organizes these as 'principles' (axioms) and 'interpretations' (theorems), drawing heavily from existing library standards and student rights statements. It addresses key areas including due process for account suspension, privacy of home directories, and the prevention of censorship in digital publications.
classification.title: Draft Statement on Computers and Academic Freedom (CAF)

identity.subject: Draft Statement on Computers and Academic Freedom (CAF)

notable_claims: The University of Waterloo banned rec.humor.funny in December 1988 following pressure from an MIT graduate student.
A university committee reported in May 1991 that administrations should not make non-financial decisions about what people can read on campus.
Dr. John McCarthy previously helped reverse a similar newsgroup ban at Stanford.
classification.summary: The University of Waterloo lifted a long-standing ban on several Usenet newsgroups, including rec.humor.funny and alt.sex, which had been implemented in 1988. The reversal followed the recommendations of a university committee that concluded administrations should not make non-financial decisions regarding content access. The process was influenced by student efforts and an invited talk by Dr. John McCarthy.
classification.title: Waterloo ban on rec.humor.funny finally lifted

identity.subject: Waterloo ban on rec.humor.funny finally lifted

notable_claims: WWU banned specific newsgroups after media coverage of pornographic files at other universities.
The WWU Vice Provost justified the ban by labeling the content as 'junk mail'.
WWU offered to reinstate groups if a professor could demonstrate a need for them.
classification.summary: Jeff Wandling reports the removal of alt.sex and alt.binary.pictures.erotica newsgroups from Western Washington University's USENET database. The action followed media reports regarding pornographic files at the University of Washington and a demotion at Central Washington University. While UofW declined to ban such material, WWU's Vice Provost for information and communication classified it as 'junk mail' to justify the ban.
classification.title: alt.sex

notable_claims: System administrators and users have fundamentally different perceptions of system robustness versus fragility.
The university's charges against Brack lacked specificity, failing to pair alleged actions with the specific rules violated.
Posting a 'fuck you' message to alt.flame is protected speech and not inherently obscene.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie critiques the disciplinary charges brought by Ohio State University's Academic Computing Services (ACS) against student Steven Brack. Kadie argues that the conflict stems from a communication breakdown between system administrators, who view systems as fragile, and users, who view them as robust boundaries to be explored. He contends that the university failed to provide due process or link specific alleged actions to violated rules.
classification.title: Re: The rules that Ohio State U. alleges that Steven Brack violated

identity.subject: Re: The rules that Ohio State U. alleges that Steven Brack violated

notable_claims: University computer file searches should be subject to the same privacy protections as physical office or dormitory spaces.
Summary suspension of computing privileges during an investigation may violate the principle of 'innocent until found guilty' and existing university codes.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie of the EFF critiques UCLA's SEASnet computing policies, arguing that they lack clarity regarding noncommercial personal use and conflict with established university search and due process standards. He advocates for aligning computer file search procedures with general campus privacy protections for students and faculty. Kadie emphasizes that users should not be suspended from computing privileges before a determination of misconduct is made.
classification.title: Re: Ucla's Use Policies

notable_claims: University newsgroup facilities are 'limited public forums' under the Public-Forum Doctrine.
Content-based prohibitions in limited public forums must be narrowly drawn to effectuate a compelling state interest.
Speech in free-speech forums like soc.women should not constitute sexual harassment.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie challenges a university administrator's decision to punish a student for posting content deemed pornographic or harassing. Kadie argues that university newsgroup facilities constitute 'limited public forums' and that the punishment violates both campus codes of conduct and First Amendment rights. He specifically disputes the claim that speech in a free-speech forum can be categorized as sexual harassment to justify censorship.
classification.title: Re: yahweh is good posting

notable_claims: Unmoderated newsgroups at universities function as free-speech forums.
Selective enforcement of newsgroup charters to punish offensive notes is prohibited by the San Diego Committee v. Governing Bd case.
Newsgroup charters are social contracts enforced by social pressure, not government policing.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie argues that unmoderated Usenet newsgroups hosted by universities should be treated as free-speech forums. He contends that newsgroup charters are social contracts rather than legally enforceable documents and that selective enforcement of such charters by state universities would be legally prohibited.
classification.title: Re: yahweh is good posting

notable_claims: System administrators may enforce viewpoint discrimination if it is codified in a newsgroup charter.
Charter enforcement is typically reactive based on complaints rather than proactive monitoring.
The admin distinguishes between free speech and the right to be free from harassment within specific digital forums.
classification.summary: An anonymous system administrator responds to queries regarding the enforcement of Usenet newsgroup charters. The admin states they would enforce charter-based viewpoint or sexual discrimination if notified of a violation, provided the group was approved by Usenet rules. They express a preference against barring users via majority vote but support removing harassment from specific forums.
classification.title: Re: off-topic notes (was yahweh is good posting)

notable_claims: The University of Illinois defines disruptive action as that which substantially impedes operations or interferes with the rights of others.
Off-topic posts are not necessarily 'substantial interference' if they can be filtered by users using kill files.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie discusses the application of University of Illinois rules regarding 'disruptive or coercive action' to network behavior. He argues that off-topic posts do not constitute substantial interference with others' rights if they can be managed via kill files. The post includes a detailed excerpt of university disciplinary codes used to define disruptive conduct.

notable_claims: Computation centers may use library policies as the basis for newsgroup access policies to preempt complaints.
classification.summary: A discussion regarding the application of library collection policies to Usenet newsgroup access at universities. John Hascall argues that computation centers should adopt existing library policies as a defensive measure against complaints about computer-material selection.
classification.title: Re: USENET censorship strikes University of Washington!

notable_claims: Anonymous FTP archives function as a new type of library.
The NSF should adopt policies based on long-standing library and academic experience to embrace free expression.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie argues that anonymous FTP archives should be treated as a new type of library and governed by established academic and library principles. He advocates for the NSF to adopt policies based on the Library Bill of Rights to protect free expression and renounce content restrictions. The post includes ALA statements on diversity in collection development to support the argument against censorship of controversial materials.
classification.title: Re: Acceptable Use Policies

notable_claims: Judge Leisure ruled CompuServe lacks editorial control over publications on its network.
Prodigy's policy of pre-screening public notes may increase its legal liability for defamatory messages.
classification.summary: A news excerpt reports on a judicial ruling stating that CompuServe is not liable for defamatory content on its network, comparing its role to that of a library or bookstore. The text contrasts this with the Prodigy network, which pre-screened messages and thus faced different liability risks. This highlights early legal distinctions between passive distributors and active moderators of online speech.
classification.title: CompuServe Isn't Liable for Contents of its Network

identity.subject: CompuServe Isn't Liable for Contents of its Network

notable_claims: System administrators in K-12 environments should control flow but not block all access to Internet services.
Supervision of youth on the net should be left to parents and instructors rather than the network provider.
classification.summary: A discussion regarding the filtering of controversial content on Usenet, specifically within K-12 educational environments. The author argues that supervision should be handled by instructors and parents rather than through systemic network censorship. The post emphasizes that blocking access to 'questionable' materials risks depriving students of valuable Internet resources.
